selections.title: 1G_Fixed Copper_Cross / 1000 / Auto/ MDI
selections.justification:
Step: Set DUT and partner device:
Speed = 1000
Duplex = Auto
Polarity = MDI / Partner device = MDI
ecofriendly lp
Connect cable to each ports lpi configured
Expected: LPI command successfully enbaled.
Confirm ports are in LPI status and configured by executing 'show ecofrienly and show interface port' command.
Check logs for appriate log messages. No error message.

selections.title: SFP Fibre-1Gig-AUTO 100/Full-Auto
selections.justification:
Step: Set DUT & partner device: Speed/Duplex = AUTO 100/Full Set Polarity settings: DUT = Auto Partner = Auto
Note: Auto 100 can be configured in x81-400 / 960. This behavior was added in the Dual Rate pluggable project: https://intranet.atlnz.lc/awpwiki/index.php/Dual_Rate_Pluggable_Support_TFS#Subsequent_Targets
Expected: Command Failure for SFP port Speed setting. Link Up Speed = 1000 Duplex & Polarity as configured
For x81-400 / 960: Commands accepted. Link Up. Speed = 100 Duplex & Polarity as configured

selections.title: SFP Copper-1Gig-Cross-MDIX/MDI
selections.justification:
Step: DUT & partner device: Speed & Duplex = Defaults Set Polarity settings: DUT = MDIX Partner = MDI
Expected: Command successful for SFP port Polarity setting. Link Down. Configured Speed and Configured Duplex set to "Auto" & Configured Polarity settings: DUT = MDIX Partner = MDI

selections.title: SFP Copper-1Gig-Straight-MDIX/MDI
selections.justification:
Step: DUT & partner device: Speed & Duplex = Defaults Set Polarity settings: DUT = MDIX Partner = MDI
Expected: Command successful. Link Up Speed, Duplex set to "Auto"
Command failure for Polarity settings: DUT = MDIX Partner = MDI (refer to CR30879)

selections.title: Configure BFD links between devices and test negotiation is succesful for differing intervals
selections.justification:
Configure BFD links between devices and test negotiation is succesful for differing intervals

[Log-derived analysis] Verifies BFD timer negotiation between peers configured with differing intervals. Confirms the session still comes up and the negotiated transmit/receive intervals resolve to the slower (highest) of the two peers' configured values, as required by the protocol.

step4.objective:
• Link established between two ports both configured for auto-negotiation, on copper and fibre media types, where supported. Speak with SVT for a list of supported tranceivers.
  • Negotiated speed and duplex equal to the highest common capability advertised by both link partners.
  • Operational status of both ports reported as up, with matching speed and duplex on each end of the link.
  • Auto-negotiation as the default administrative setting on ports that support it, present after a fresh start with no explicit configuration.
  • Negotiated operational values distinguishable from configured values in the reported port state, with negotiation mode shown as auto/enabled.
  • Re-negotiation performed after link loss, cable reconnection, port disable/enable, or device restart, returning the same negotiated result.
  • Updated negotiated speed and duplex after a link partner's advertised capabilities change, without requiring manual intervention.
  • Auto-negotiation on a port whose partner is fixed-configured resolving to a link at a compatible speed, with duplex behaviour consistent with the platform's fallback rules.
  • No link, or a clearly reported fault state, when the two ends share no common capability.
  • Fibre ports negotiating in line with the capabilities of the inserted transceiver, including after transceiver removal and insertion of a different type.
  • Link state and negotiation transitions recorded in logs and available through statistics, counters, and management interfaces.
  • No unexpected link flapping, error counter growth, or resource leakage across repeated negotiation cycles.

provenance.objective_response:
• Link established between two ports both configured for auto-negotiation, on copper and fibre media types.
  • Negotiated speed and duplex equal to the highest common capability advertised by both link partners.
  • Full-duplex selected in preference to half-duplex where both partners advertise both modes at the negotiated speed.
  • MDI/MDI-X crossover resolved automatically, with link up over both straight-through and crossover cabling.
  • Operational status of both ports reported as up, with matching speed and duplex on each end of the link.
  • Traffic forwarded without loss or error at the negotiated speed and duplex in both directions.
  • Auto-negotiation as the default administrative setting on ports that support it, present after a fresh start with no explicit configuration.
  • Negotiated operational values distinguishable from configured values in the reported port state, with negotiation mode shown as auto/enabled.
  • Re-negotiation performed after link loss, cable reconnection, port disable/enable, or device restart, returning the same negotiated result.
  • Updated negotiated speed and duplex after a link partner's advertised capabilities change, without requiring manual intervention.
  • Auto-negotiation on a port whose partner is fixed-configured resolving to a link at a compatible speed, with duplex behaviour consistent with the platform's fallback rules.
  • No link, or a clearly reported fault state, when the two ends share no common capability.
  • Rejection or clear error reporting when auto-negotiation is requested on a port or transceiver type that does not support it, with the prior port state preserved.
  • Fibre ports negotiating in line with the capabilities of the inserted transceiver, including after transceiver removal and insertion of a different type.
  • Negotiation result unchanged by unrelated configuration changes on the port or device.
  • Link state and negotiation transitions recorded in logs and available through statistics, counters, and management interfaces.
  • Notifications or events raised on link up, link down, and change of negotiated speed or duplex.
  • Consistent negotiated values reported across all management interfaces exposing port state.
  • No unexpected link flapping, error counter growth, or resource leakage across repeated negotiation cycles.

steps.description: Note: Related ART Tests linked in Traceability.

With a fresh start and no explicit port configuration applied, inspect the administrative negotiation setting on ports that support auto-negotiation across the available media types. Confirm auto-negotiation is the default state and that the reported port state distinguishes the configured setting from the operational result.

Connect the DUT to a link partner on a port with both ends set to auto-negotiation using a fibre port and a supported transceiver, selecting transceiver types from the list agreed with SVT so that more than one supported speed grade is exercised. Confirm the link establishes and the negotiated values are consistent with the inserted transceiver's capabilities.
Establish an auto/auto link using crossover copper cabling. Confirm the link comes up, that the negotiated speed and duplex match on both ends, and that the resolved MDI/MDIX polarity is reported.

Repeat the copper auto/auto link with straight-through cabling in place of crossover. Confirm polarity is resolved automatically and the same negotiated speed and duplex result is reached as with crossover cabling.

Restrict the capabilities advertised by the link partner so that the highest common capability is below the maximum either port can support, covering a lower speed and a half-duplex case where the platform supports it. Confirm the negotiated speed and duplex settle on the highest capability common to both ends rather than the port maximum.

On an established auto/auto link, force re-negotiation by each of the available means in turn — removing and restoring the cable, administratively disabling and re-enabling the port, and restarting the device. Confirm the link re-establishes in each case and the negotiated speed, duplex and polarity return to the same values as before.

While an auto/auto link is up, change the capabilities advertised by the link partner to a different speed or duplex grade without touching the DUT configuration. Confirm the DUT updates its negotiated speed and duplex to the new highest common capability with no manual intervention on the DUT.

Leave the DUT port on auto-negotiation while fixing the link partner to a specific speed and duplex, covering both a matching-speed and a differing-speed partner setting. Confirm the resulting link state and duplex behaviour follow the platform's documented fallback rules and that the reported operational values reflect what was actually resolved.

Configure the two ends so that they share no common speed or duplex capability. Confirm no link is brought up, or that a fault state is clearly reported, and that the port does not flap between states while the mismatch persists.

With a fibre port in an auto/auto configuration, remove the transceiver and insert a different supported type with different capabilities, then return to the original. Confirm the port re-negotiates to values in line with each inserted transceiver and that removal and insertion are reported in the port state.

Across the link-up, link-loss and re-negotiation events exercised above, review the logging, statistics, counters and management interfaces available on the platform. Confirm link state and negotiation transitions are recorded consistently and that the negotiated values are reported identically across the available management paths.

Cycle the link repeatedly through negotiation over a sustained run on both copper and fibre ports. Confirm the negotiated result is consistent on every cycle, that no unexpected flapping or error counter growth occurs, and that device resource usage does not trend upward across the run.

## TestLink selections (evidence — reuse their concrete values where they fit) - AWP-12283: 1G_Fixed Copper_Cross / 1000 / Auto/ MDI - AWP-108: SFP Fibre-1Gig-AUTO 100/Full-Auto - AWP-98: SFP Copper-1Gig-Cross-MDIX/MDI - AWP-87: SFP Copper-1Gig-Straight-MDIX/MDI ## Zephyr exemplars (evidence — match their level of detail) - AWPTCM-T46849: interface: port status, speed, duplex and negotiation - AWPTCM-T33889: TQrouter - Basic function: auto negotiation on ethernet ports - AWPTCM-T32632: IE220 Device Management - Auto-negotiation #127 - AWPTCM-T31152: Profinet: Hardware; Check of Auto-Negotiation ## ATPyLib coverage (selected ART) - 1360.1001.3: Configure BFD links between devices and test negotiation is succesful for differing intervals ## Known coverage gaps The selected ART coverage (1360.1001.3) exercises negotiation only in the BFD session sense — establishing links between devices and confirming session parameters converge across differing interval settings — so it provides confidence in protocol-level negotiation and link stability, but it is a poor proxy for the physical-layer Auto/Auto behaviour this case targets. Not addressed by automation are copper and fibre PHY auto-negotiation outcomes across speed and duplex combinations (including forced 1000/Auto and Auto 100/Full pairings), MDI/MDIX polarity resolution on straight and crossed cabling for both native copper and SFP-based ports, and mismatch or fallback cases where DUT and partner advertise differing capabilities. Observability of the resulting negotiated state — port status, resolved speed, duplex and polarity as reported by the platform, and link transitions on renegotiation or cable reconnection — is likewise absent, as is any coverage of energy-efficient/LPI interaction with negotiation. The related Zephyr cross-references (AWPTCM-T46849, T33889, T32632, T31152) indicate this behaviour is validated elsewhere on a per-platform basis, but no equivalent automated check exists in the ART suite for this case, leaving the "covered by auto-test" claim weakly supported. ## Rules - The FIRST step is injected server-side as a traceability note — DO NOT generate it. - Generate ONLY the subsequent verification steps exercising the objective's artefacts. - Cover each major objective bullet: positive, negative, special conditions, reporting. - Keep each step high-level enough to be reusable across platforms, but specific enough to be testable. Naming exact values, counts and timings is the PyTest script's job, not this one — a manual step that dictates them narrows the tester to one way of exercising the feature instead of leaving them to produce evidence that it works. - LEAVE `expectedResult` EMPTY on every step. This is deliberate, not an omission. The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Proving the step was taken — capturing `show` output as evidence — is the generated PyTest script's job, and naming commands or device registers here invents mechanisms that may not exist and narrows the tester besides. - Where a step depends on topology, say which roles it needs (e.g. two links between the DUT and a partner), never a device model or a port number. - Platform-agnostic language: no product names, no hardcoded port strings. ## Output format — this example IS the specification; match its level of detail [ { "description": "Verify LLDP operation with the DUT and its link partner both running default timers. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.
